heading_path: Chapter 3: HIV Testing Services > Summary of Changes
text:
### **SUMMARY OF CHANGES** | **2022 GUIDANCE** | **2024 GUIDANCE** | | --- | --- | | Training of HTS counsellors to be conducted by PSI and TASC | • Any accredited institution recognized by SNAP and EHLS may train HTS Counsellors
• Entry requirements for HTS training is completion of Form V | | The HIV testing screening tool will be used to determine eligibility for HTS. | • HIVST replaces the risk based HTS screening tool in all individuals 12 years and above (excluding clients eligible for routine testing).
• Routine testing following the National HIV Testing Algorithm should be offered to malnourished and sick children, HIV-exposed children, clients with confirmed or presumptive TB disease, STI clients, index contacts and inpatient, pregnant and lactating women and KPs. | | Use the HIV screening tool for children and adolescents (6-15yrs) to determine eligibility for HTS. | • All children 2-11 years utilize the paediatric HIV screening tool in all entry points unless they qualify for routine testing | | HIV Self-test kits/Oraquick can be distributed at the health facility level and performed privately in the client’s home or facilitated by a healthcare worker in a private setting at a health facility. | • The age of consent for HIVST has been reduced from 16 years to 12 years |

### **SUMMARY OF CHANGES**

| **2022 GUIDANCE** | **2024 GUIDANCE** |
| --- | --- |
| Training of HTS counsellors to be conducted by PSI and TASC | • Any accredited institution recognized by SNAP and EHLS may train HTS Counsellors / • Entry requirements for HTS training is completion of Form V |
| The HIV testing screening tool will be used to determine eligibility for HTS. | • HIVST replaces the risk based HTS screening tool in all individuals 12 years and above (excluding clients eligible for routine testing). / • Routine testing following the National HIV Testing Algorithm should be offered to malnourished and sick children, HIV-exposed children, clients with confirmed or presumptive TB disease, STI clients, index contacts and inpatient, pregnant and lactating women and KPs. |
| Use the HIV screening tool for children and adolescents (6-15yrs) to determine eligibility for HTS. | • All children 2-11 years utilize the paediatric HIV screening tool in all entry points unless they qualify for routine testing |
| HIV Self-test kits/Oraquick can be distributed at the health facility level and performed privately in the client’s home or facilitated by a healthcare worker in a private setting at a health facility. | • The age of consent for HIVST has been reduced from 16 years to 12 years |

narrative: HIV eligibility screening process flow for a patient arriving at the facility (Amendment 2024, section 3.2 HIV screening tools). Ask whether the patient has ever been tested for HIV. If never tested, refer to the HTS counsellor for risk assessment (children 2-11 years) or HIVST screening (children 12 years and above, adolescents and adults). If tested before, ask the status. If the status is negative, refer to the HTS counsellor as above. text:
| 1. Use of HIV-ST among PrEP Clients |
| --- |
| There are two key approaches where HIVST can be considered as part of PrEP delivery: |
| **1. Demand generation and linkage to PrEP:** HIVST can be an important tool to generate demand for PrEP by reaching individuals who may not otherwise test or access health facilities. |
| **2. PrEP (re-)initiation and follow-up visits:** HIVST can be used for clients (re-)initiating or continuing oral PrEP or the PrEP ring. For \*\*CAB-LA users\*\*, a National HIV Testing Algorithm **needs to be used.** |

• Client wants to continue with the same PrEP method,

• If positive to discontinue their PrEP method and report to the facility for confirmation of the test result and linkage to ART.

narrative: Status-neutral HIV prevention and care approach (Amendment 2024, section 4.1). Everyone starts with an HIV test. A negative result leads to the prevention pathway, which prevents getting HIV: people are offered powerful prevention tools such as PrEP, condoms, harm reduction (for example syringe services programmes) and supportive services to stay HIV negative; components are high-impact HIV prevention and HIV and STD testing. A positive result leads to the treatment pathway, which prevents transmitting HIV: people enter primary care and are offered effective treatment and supportive services to achieve and maintain viral suppression; components are effective treatment and HIV primary care. A person on the prevention pathway who is newly diagnosed with HIV moves to the treatment pathway. Both pathways share culturally inclusive and responsive quality care, and prevention and treatment of syndemic infections.

## SUMMARY OF CHANGES | 2022 GUIDANCE | 2024 GUIDANCE | | --- | --- | | | • Pretreatment VL for all newly diagnosed clients initiating ART. Clients returning to care should not receive PTVL | | • The first routine VL test is to be done by 6 months post-ART initiation | • The first routine VL test is to be done 3 months post-ART initiation. Ensure that all clients have a VL test done BY 6 months of starting ART | | • The 2nd routine VL test should be done 6 months after an initial suppressed VL test result | • The 2nd routine VL test should be done 6 months after an initial suppressed VL test result and then annually thereafter. For children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, it should be done every 6 months | | • 3MMD can be started after a suppressed VL done 6 months following ART initiation | • Up to 3MMD of ARVs can be started after an initial suppressed VL test results done at 3 months
• Up to 6MMD can be given following 2 consecutive suppressed VL test results | | | • Remnant blood samples of all infants who test HIV positive may be stored and used for surveillance purposes (plasma or DBS) for HIVDR survey activities | | | • Routine HIVDR testing for all PrEP breakthrough infections |

ART-naive client: do baseline laboratory tests including pre-treatment viral load (PTVL) and initiate ART. Treatment-experienced client: do baseline laboratory tests excluding PTVL and re-initiate the previous regimen. Follow-up VL at 3 months after ART initiation: if VL is below 200 copies/mL, the client is eligible for up to 3 months of multi-month dispensing (MMD); if VL is above 200 copies/mL, refer to SUAC. For treatment-experienced clients with VL below 200 copies/mL, continue the current ART regimen; eligible for up to 3MMD. Follow-up VL at 9 months after ART initiation: if VL is below 200 copies/mL, the client is eligible for MMD and differentiated service delivery (DSD) enrolment, and for treatment-experienced clients up to 6MMD and DSD enrolment; if VL is above 200 copies/mL, see the management of low-level viraemia (LLV). After a suppressed VL, continue routine VL monitoring thereafter.

text:
## **CHAPTER 8: PREVENTION OF MOTHER TO-CHILD TRANSMISSION OF HIV**

### **SUMMARY OF CHANGES**

| **2022 GUIDANCE** | **2024 GUIDANCE** |
| --- | --- |
| Genotypes were recommended for pregnant or breastfeeding women failing a DTG or PI based ART regimen. | Updated guidance provides more details for same day clinical care decisions and consideration of empiric therapy for women deemed highest risk while awaiting genotype results. Emphasis is placed on intensive adherence interventions for all women with a DVL >50. |
| No specific recommendations for breastfeeding infants of mothers found to have seroconverted. | 3 drug PEP after appropriate testing is recommended for breastfeeding infants of mothers found to have seroconverted. |
| Repeat VL 1 month after SUAC | Specific recommendation to consult the DR committee for all women who remain with VL > 50 despite 1 month of intensive adherence support. |

Sections: Empiric Therapy
- Pregnant Woman with VL> 50 c/mL -> VL 50-1000 c/mL; DTG <18/12; DTG >18/12 or unknown
- VL 50-1000 c/mL; DTG <18/12 -> INTENSIVE ADHERENCE INTERVENTIONS; 1. DOT; 2. Mentor mother/EC involvement; 3. F/U VL 1/12; 4. If VL remains >1000 or if VL remains 50-1000 consult DR committee
- DTG >18/12 or unknown -> Genotype if VL>1000*
- Genotype if VL>1000* -> Send genotypes same day (unless known default or very poor adherence in first trimester). Complete and submit a genotype motivation requested to snapthirdline@mohcoag.org; 1st DVL in 1st trimester or 2nd trimester; 1st DVL in 3rd trimester OR 2nd DVL in any trimester
- 1st DVL in 1st trimester or 2nd trimester -> INTENSIVE ADHERENCE INTERVENTIONS; 1. DOT; 2. Mentor mother/EC involvement; 3. F/U VL 1/12; 4. If VL remains >1000 or if VL remains 50-1000 consult DR committee
- 1st DVL in 3rd trimester OR 2nd DVL in any trimester -> Prior PI
- *Provide the same intensive adherence interventions as outlined in the yellow box to the left -> 1st DVL in 3rd trimester OR 2nd DVL in any trimester
- Prior PI -> (No) TLD 1 TAB OD PLUS EITHER DRV/R (400/50) 2 tabs od* OR ATV/R (300/50) 1 tab od *if available; (Yes) TLD 1 TAB OD PLUS DRV/R (600/100) BD
- When the baby is born -> 2 drug EIP X6/52 and then NVP only minimum 14/52 and mother is documented undetectable. Consider 3 drug ART for babies born to women with seroconversion at delivery, perform 2 tests prior to initiation. VL at delivery for all women. Birth test all infants. Please consult for PLW with viremia on concurrent ATT.

narrative: Same-day management of viraemia (detectable viral load, DVL) in pregnant women (Amendment 2024, chapter 8, PMTCT). Applies to a pregnant woman with VL above 50 c/mL. If VL is 50-1000 c/mL and she has been on dolutegravir (DTG) for less than 18 months, start intensive adherence interventions: directly observed therapy (DOT), mentor mother or expert client (EC) involvement, repeat VL in 1 month, and if VL remains above 1000, or remains 50-1000, consult the drug resistance (DR) committee. If she has been on DTG for more than 18 months or the duration is unknown, do a genotype if VL is above 1000; send genotypes the same day (unless known default or very poor adherence in the first trimester) and submit a genotype motivation to the third-line email address. First DVL in the first or second trimester: give the intensive adherence interventions. First DVL in the third trimester, or second DVL in any trimester: ask about prior protease inhibitor (PI) use. No prior PI: empiric therapy TLD 1 tablet daily plus either DRV/r 400/50 mg 2 tablets daily or ATV/r 300/50 mg 1 tablet daily (if available). Prior PI: TLD 1 tablet daily plus DRV/r 600/100 mg twice daily. When the baby is born: 2-drug infant prophylaxis (EIP) for 6 weeks, then NVP only until at least 14 weeks and the mother is documented undetectable; consider 3-drug ART for babies of women who seroconvert at delivery (2 tests before initiation); VL at delivery for all women; birth test all infants; consult for viraemia with concurrent TB treatment.

narrative: Same-day management of viraemia (detectable viral load, DVL) in breastfeeding women (Amendment 2024, chapter 5). First test the infant immediately; if reactive, initiate ART as soon as possible; if non-reactive, follow the algorithm below; consider presumptive ART for all HIV-exposed infants who appear ill or have failure to thrive while awaiting results. For the mother with VL 50-1000 c/mL on TLD1 or TLD2 with DTG for less than 18 months: intensive adherence interventions (DOT, mentor mother or expert client involvement, repeat VL in 1 month, and if VL stays above 1000 or stays 50-1000 consult the DR committee). If on DTG for more than 18 months or unknown: genotype if VL is above 1000, sent the same day, with a genotype motivation to the third-line email address. First DVL: intensive adherence interventions. Second DVL: discuss AFASS (acceptable, feasible, affordable, sustainable, safe) and proceed if breastfeeding is ongoing; ask about prior protease inhibitor (PI) use. No prior PI: empiric therapy TLD 1 tablet daily plus DRV/r 400/50 mg 2 tablets daily or ATV/r 300/50 mg 1 tablet daily (if available). Prior PI: TLD 1 tablet daily plus DRV/r 600/100 mg twice daily. Also follow the list on caring for the breastfeeding child.

heading_path: Chapter 5: Basic Care Package for HIV-Positive Individuals > Same Day Management of Viremia in Breastfeeding Women
text:
**Caring for the breastfeeding child**

* If child is <6/52: Continue EIP (AT/NVP)
* If child is >6/52: Continue or restart NVP until the mother is undetectable
* If AFASS criteria are met and mother prefers wean after clear discussion of risks and benefits, advise wean.
* Follow a weaned infant monthly for weight check
* If mother acutely seroconverted, test infant. If negative consider PEP in baby until mom is undetectable

heading_path: Chapter 9: ART for Children & Adolescents > Summary of Changes
text:
### **SUMMARY OF CHANGES**

| **2022 GUIDANCE** | **2024 GUIDANCE** |
| --- | --- |
| **9.3:** Omitted | Any ill-appearing HIV exposed infant should start ART ***presumptively*** while awaiting results. |
| **9.6:** No mention of pALD (+ Annex) | **pALD** included in the new paediatric dosing chart |
| **9.8:** Missing TPT dosing for CALHIV | ***Dosing chart included for TPT*** in CALHIV |
| **9.9:** Spelling correction in table | Spelling corrected for NRTI |
| **9.10:** Clinical Monitoring of Children and Adolescents on ART: MMD guidance change | All children stable on ART >1-2 years may receive up to 3MMD, and all ***children stable on ART >2 years may receive up to 6 MMD.*** |
| **9.11:** 3 months VL was a substitute test | ***Baseline and 3-month VL test are additional tests.*** This will align with the CWF visits and support service integration. |
| **9.12:** Second Line ART revised to remove: “Refer to National HIVDR Clinical Expert Committee if on DTG for < 2 years” | Align with adult guidance and highlight ***all*** PI and DTG treatment failures will require ***genotype guided switches***. “HIV resistance testing should be done for all clients failing on a DTG based ART regimen. Only switch to 2nd line if resistance test shows DTG resistance and the 2nd line regimen should be a boosted PI + 2 NRTIs determined by the genotype results”. ***(From Table 7.11 Recommended Sequence of Second Line NRTI Options)*** |

text:
1 Although children younger than 5 years are defined as having Advanced HIV Disease at presentation, those who have been receiving ART >1 year and who are clinically stable (reliable caregiver, undetectable viral load, no OI’s, normal growth curve, normal development, appropriately immunized for age, stable vital signs), should not be considered to have advanced disease and should be eligible/have the option for multi-month dispensing. Multi-month (MMD) refills should include prophylaxis (CTX, TPT). Family-centered care should be implemented and ART care appointments for the mother and their babies should be linked to the mother-baby pair visit schedules. text:
### **NCD Risk Factors**

| Category | Risk Factor | Clinical Relevance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Non-Modifiable | Age | Risk increases significantly after age 40, especially for DM and HTN. |
| Non-Modifiable | Gender | Specific risks (e.g., gender-specific cancers, cardiovascular disease patterns). |
| Non-Modifiable | Family History | Genetic predisposition to HTN, DM, or premature coronary artery disease (CAD). |
| Modifiable | Overweight/Obesity | High BMI is a primary driver for HTN and DM. |
| Modifiable | Tobacco Use (Smoking) | A leading preventable cause of cardiovascular and chronic respiratory diseases and lung cancer. |
| Modifiable | Alcohol Use | Increases risk of liver disease, some cancers, and hypertension. |
| Modifiable | Unhealthy Diet | High intake of salt, sugar, and saturated fats contributes to hypertension and dyslipidaemia and some cancers. |
| Modifiable | Lack of Physical Activity | A sedentary lifestyle is a key independent risk factor for all major NCDs. |

heading_path: Chapter 1: Prevention, Health Education and Routine Health Examinations > Risk Factor Assessment Algorithms > Blood Pressure Screening Algorithm
text:
### **Blood Pressure Screening Algorithm**

| BP Reading (mmHg) | Category | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <120/80 | **Normal** | Recheck in 1 year or at next clinic visit whichever comes first; promote healthy lifestyle |
| 120-129/<80 | **Elevated** | Lifestyle modification; recheck in 3-6 months |
| 130-139/80-89 | **Stage 1 Hypertension** | Confirm with 2 more readings; initiate lifestyle + medication if CVD risk ≥10% |
| ≥140/90 | **Stage 2 Hypertension** | Confirm within 1 month; initiate lifestyle + medication |
| ≥180/120 | **Hypertensive Crisis** | **URGENT: Assess for end-organ damage; immediate treatment** |

| ≥180/120 | **Hypertensive Crisis** | **URGENT: Assess for end-organ damage; immediate treatment** |

narrative: Smoking and nicotine cessation approach (NCDIMH guidelines, page 19). Ask: do you smoke, do you know the risks, have you thought of quitting? Alert: do you know the benefits of quitting and that we can help? Assess: is the client ready to quit? If no or maybe, give a motivational pamphlet, encourage follow-up and ask again at the next visit. If yes, arrange a cessation intervention and review nicotine dependence (Fagerstrom score or CO levels, current smoking and quit-attempt history, social stressors and household smokers). Motivated with low dependence: may manage with counselling and support alone or nicotine replacement therapy (NRT); offer support groups and text, internet or smartphone-based support. Motivated with high dependence: probably needs added pharmacological support; assess medical and psychiatric history, ability to purchase medicine and medication availability. Then set a quit date and arrange support and medication if needed; options are NRT (patch, gum, spray), varenicline and bupropion. Follow up: assess withdrawal symptoms and drug side effects, evaluate mood and psychosocial stressors, identify relapse potential.

| • Quitting alcohol improves your health at any age |
| • You don't have to quit alone - ask for help from healthcare providers, family, and support groups |
| • If you are pregnant or planning pregnancy, do **NOT** drink any alcohol |

Diagram: Algorithm for Diabetes Mellitus Screening (section: Algorithm for Diabetes Mellitus Screening)
- All clients >18 years attending a health facility should be screened for diabetes using these known risk factors. See table on the right -> NO Re-evaluate; YES Test

narrative: Algorithm for diabetes mellitus screening (NCDIMH guidelines, page 28). All clients older than 18 years attending a health facility should be screened for diabetes using known risk factors. If no risk factors, re-evaluate later. If risk factors are present, test with haemoglobin A1C (HbA1c), fasting plasma glucose, oral glucose tolerance test or random glucose test. Normal result (HbA1c below 5.7%, fasting glucose below 100 mg/dL): encourage a healthy lifestyle and retest at least annually. Prediabetes (HbA1c 5.6-6.4%, glucose 100-125 mg/dL, or 140-199 mg/dL on the glucose tolerance test): encourage lifestyle modification and retest every 6-12 months. Diabetes range (HbA1c 6.5% or more, fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or more): retest with a different test and refer for treatment if still positive.

narrative: Lipid management clinical decision pathway (NCDIMH guidelines, page 29). Obtain a fasting lipid profile at baseline and annually. Then do three things. First, calculate and categorise cardiovascular (CV) risk with the Framingham Risk Score: low risk below 10%, moderate 10-19%, high above 20%. Second, assess comorbidities: diabetes, coronary artery disease (CAD), previous CV event, atherosclerosis or aneurysm; any one of these means high risk. Third, determine lipid targets. LDL-C: optimal below 100 mg/dL, near or above optimal 100-129, borderline high 130-159, high 160-189, very high 190 or more. Total cholesterol: desirable below 200 mg/dL, borderline high 200-239, high 240 or more. Triglycerides: normal below 150 mg/dL, borderline high 150-199, high 200-499, very high 500 or more. All three feed into treating to the target.

Diagram: Chronic Kidney Disease Clinical Protocols (section: Chronic Kidney Disease Clinical Protocols)
Items: TRACE PROTEIN ON URINE DIPSTICK
- Offer a Kidney Health Check to people with • Diabetes • Hypertension • Established CVD • Family history of kidney failure • Obesity (BMI ≥30) • Current or past smoker / vaper • History of AKI aged ≥60 years • High index of suspicion in clients esp paedes with edema and recurrent puffiness -> uACR ≥3 mg/mmol; eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m
- uACR ≥3 mg/mmol -> Yes
- eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m -> No; Yes
- Yes -> Repeat uACR within 3 months. If uACR normal, complete a third test (preferably first morning void)
- Yes -> Repeat eGFR within 7 days
- No -> Repeat Kidney Health Check (annually if aged ≥18, people with diabetes or hypertension)
- Repeat eGFR within 7 days -> If ≥20% reduction in eGFR, possible AKI. Discuss with nephrologist; Repeat eGFR within 3 months
- Repeat uACR within 3 months. If uACR normal, complete a third test (preferably first morning void) -> If minimum of two uACRs ≥3 mg/mmol over 3 months
- Repeat eGFR within 3 months -> If minimum of two eGFRs <60mL/min.1.73m2
- If minimum of two uACRs ≥3 mg/mmol over 3 months -> and/or
- If minimum of two eGFRs <60mL/min.1.73m2 -> and/or

narrative: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) clinical protocol: kidney health check (NCDIMH guidelines, page 29). Offer a kidney health check to people with diabetes, hypertension, established cardiovascular disease, family history of kidney failure, obesity (BMI 30 or more), current or past smoking or vaping, history of acute kidney injury (AKI) aged 60 or more, or a high index of suspicion (especially children with oedema and recurrent puffiness). Tests: urine albumin-creatinine ratio (uACR) of 3 mg/mmol or more, trace protein on urine dipstick, and eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73m2. If eGFR is 60 or more, repeat the kidney health check (annually if aged 18 or more, or with diabetes or hypertension). If uACR is raised, repeat uACR within 3 months; if normal, do a third test (preferably first morning void). If eGFR is below 60, repeat eGFR within 7 days (a reduction of 20% or more suggests possible AKI; discuss with a nephrologist) and again within 3 months. CKD is confirmed if at least two uACRs are 3 mg/mmol or more over 3 months and/or at least two eGFRs are below 60. Then stage CKD using the staging table with eGFR and uACR.

narrative: Algorithm for chronic kidney disease (CKD) screening (NCDIMH guidelines, page 30). Target population with risk factors (high blood pressure, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, family history, HIV): screen with urine dipstick, blood glucose, blood pressure and family history, and measure kidney function (serum creatinine and estimated GFR). Population with no markers of risk: do not screen. Determine whether results indicate CKD (eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73m2 or albuminuria). If not, rescreen based on risks. Whether or not CKD is present, the management package is: lifestyle modification (smoking cessation, balanced diet, regular exercise, salt below 2 g/day); medical treatment of diabetes, blood pressure and lipids (SGLT2 inhibitors, ACEI/ARB, statins, metformin); considerations (drug dosing, contrast media, CKD complications such as anaemia, hyperkalaemia, bone disease, CVD); then retesting, follow-up visits and referral to nephrology when appropriate.

text:
# CHAPTER 2

## Diabetes

| **Definition:** Diabetes Mellitus is a chronic metabolic condition in which the pancreas no longer produces enough insulin (impaired insulin secretion) or cells stop responding to the insulin that is produced (insulin resistance) resulting in increased blood glucose. |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Classification** |  |  |
| **Common types** 1. **Type 1 diabetes:** due to autoimmune b-cell destruction, usually leading to absolute insulin deficiency including latent autoimmune diabetes of adulthood) 2. **Type 2 diabetes:** due to a progressive loss of b-cell insulin secretion frequently on the background of insulin resistance) | **Specific types of diabetes:** - **Monogenic diabetes syndromes:** ✓ Neonatal diabetes ✓ Maturity-onset diabetes of the young - Diseases of the exocrine pancreas (such as cystic fibrosis and pancreatitis) - **Drug-or chemical-induced diabetes:** glucocorticoid use, treatment of HIV/AIDS, or after organ transplantation - **Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM):** diabetes diagnosed in the second or third trimester of pregnancy that was not clearly overt diabetes before gestation. |  |
| **Treatment Target** |  |  |
| HbA1c <7% for most adults - HbA1c <6.5% for type 1 diabetes without hypoglycemia - HbA1c <8% for people with frequent hypoglycemia, limited life expectancy, cardiovascular complications. | All clients on treatment should aim for a glycemia (random or fasting ranging: 5-10mmol/L |  |

text:
Diagram: Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Outpatient (section: Type 2 Diabetes Pharmacological Treatment)
- Newly Diagnosed Type 2 DM patient, check HbA1c -> Health promotion (disease, medication adherence, nutrition, behaviour) individual and group
- Health promotion (disease, medication adherence, nutrition, behaviour) individual and group -> HbA1c <7%; HbA1c <7%-8%; HbA1c <8%-9.9%; HbA1c >10%
- HbA1c <7% -> Lifestyle modification Recheck HbA1c in 6 months
- HbA1c <7%-8% -> Start Metformin1 1. 500 mg OD 2. Recheck HbA1c in 3 months 3. Increase dose every 3 months until at goal or maximum tolerated dose

narrative: Outpatient pharmacological management of type 2 diabetes (T2DM) (NCDIMH guidelines, page 34). T2DM is diagnosed with fasting plasma glucose above 7.0 mmol/L or random glucose above 11.1 mmol/L, needing two positive tests, one being fasting. For a newly diagnosed patient, check HbA1c and give health promotion (disease, adherence, nutrition, behaviour). HbA1c below 7%: lifestyle modification and recheck HbA1c in 6 months. HbA1c 7-8%: start metformin 500 mg daily, recheck HbA1c in 3 months, increase dose every 3 months to goal or maximum tolerated dose. HbA1c 8-9.9%: consider dual therapy; metformin 500 mg daily titrated every 2 weeks to a maximum of 2 g, plus a second drug (sulfonylurea, DPP-4 inhibitor, pioglitazone, GLP-1 agonist or SGLT-2 inhibitor). HbA1c above 10%: consider insulin alone or with metformin (consult physician), starting low and increasing to target. Follow-up: if HbA1c is below 7%, continue medication, recheck HbA1c in 6 months and fasting glucose every 3 months; if above 7%, add a second oral agent, recheck in 3 months and increase until target or maximum dose; if HbA1c remains above 8%, review with a physician and consider referral to the diabetes clinic for insulin. For older patients an HbA1c goal below 8% is reasonable. Metformin and kidney function: do not start if CrCl is below 45 mL/min; continue if already on it with CrCl 30-45 but repeat CrCl in 6 months; stop if CrCl is below 30.

text:
**T2DM Diagnosis Criteria**
1. FPG > 7.0 mmol/L
2. Random glucose > 11.1 mmol/L
3. Need two positive tests, one must be FBG

**For older patients, it is reasonable to set the HbA1c goal at < 8%**

**<sup>1</sup>Caution: Metformin use in Patients with reduced kidney function**
1. Do not start new patients on metformin if CrCl < 45 ml /min
2. Continue metformin if already on it and CrCl is 30-45ml/min but repeat CrCl in 6 months
3. Stop metformin if CrCl < 30ml/min

narrative: Stepwise approach to insulin initiation in type 2 diabetes (NCDIMH guidelines, page 38). Step 1, basal insulin (usually with metformin): start 10 units daily or 0.1-0.2 units/kg/day; adjust by 10-15% or 2-4 units once or twice weekly to reach the fasting glucose target; for hypoglycaemia, find and address the cause and reduce the dose by 4 units or 10-20%. Step 2, if not controlled after the fasting target is reached (or the basal dose exceeds 0.5 units/kg/day), treat postprandial excursions with mealtime insulin (consider a GLP-1 receptor agonist trial first): either add 1 rapid-acting insulin injection before the largest meal (start 4 units, 0.1 units/kg or 10% of basal dose; if A1C is below 8%, consider reducing basal by the same amount; increase by 1-2 units or 10-15% once or twice weekly until the self-monitored glucose target; for hypoglycaemia reduce by 2-4 units or 10-20%), or change to premixed insulin twice daily (divide the basal dose 2/3 morning and 1/3 evening, or half and half; same adjustment rules). Step 3, if still not controlled, consider basal-bolus: add 2 or more rapid-acting injections before the largest meals, starting 4 units, 0.1 units/kg or 10% of basal dose per meal, with the same adjustment rules.

narrative: Diagnosis of type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) (NCDIMH guidelines, page 40). Symptoms such as weight loss, polyuria and polydipsia, or increased risk of diabetes, lead to suspecting diabetes. Diagnostic thresholds: fasting plasma glucose 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or more, random plasma glucose 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or more, or HbA1c 6.5% or more. In case of abnormal plasma glucose values, experts suggest an HbA1c as a useful baseline. Immune-mediated diabetes is identified by the presence of autoimmune markers, tested in tertiary care: islet cell autoantibodies and autoantibodies to GAD (GAD65), insulin, the tyrosine phosphatases IA-2 and IA-2 beta, and ZnT8.

text:
### **Basal-bolus regimen (PREFERRED REGIMEN)**

Short acting insulin 15 - 30 minutes before a meal or rapid acting insulin with main meals e.g. breakfast, lunch and main evening meal; intermediate acting insulin before bed.

* Normally, 30 - 40% of the total daily dose of insulin is given at bedtime as intermediate acting insulin. The remaining insulin is given prior to breakfast, lunch and evening meal in the form of short acting insulin.

text:
## **OR**

* Two injections daily.
* A mixture (premixed combination) of short and intermediate acting insulins (before breakfast and the main evening meal).
* The total daily dose is divided so that 2/3 is given in the morning and 1/3 in the evening.
* The morning or evening dose is then again split between the intermediate-acting and the short-acting insulin in a 70:30 ratio which is pre-mixed.
* The regimen is less flexible, but it is easier to give administration instructions

text:
| **Management of Diabetic Emergencies** | | | --- | --- | | Based on clinical evaluation and immediate bedside investigations. Features include polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, abdominal pain, fruity odor, confusion, Kussmaul breathing, dehydration

**Diabetic Ketoacidosis**
• Hyperglycemia: BG >13.9mmol/L
• Euglycemia<250mg/dl (pregnancy, SGLT2 use)
• Ketonuria or ketonemia(>3mmol/L): highly positive
• Acidosis pH: <7.3, low HCO3- :<10 ≤ 15 mEq/L
• Anion gap: >12(see formula)

**Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State**
• Severe Hyperglycemia: BG:>600>1000 mg/dl 33.3mmol/L
• Hyperosmolality: Effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg (see formula)
• Neurologic signs: focal signs, obtundation, seizure, coma | • Vital signs, volume status (decreased skin turgor, dry axillae & oral mucosa, low JVP, tachycardia and hypotension), mental status
• Immediately: serum blood glucose, urine ketones
• Additional testing: FBC, electrolytes, FT, ABG
• Evaluate for precipitating causes: SEPTIC SCREEN (urinalysis, blood cultures), cardiac enzymes, ECG, CXR
• Pregnancy test if indicated

**Monitoring**
• **BG hourly**
• **Urinary ketones and serum pH for DKA and Serum Osms for HHS 4hourly**
• **Electrolytes, primarily Na+ and K+ 4hourly**
• Mental status: expect improvement with treatment if DKA or HHS are the causes. Consider further evaluation if not improving
• Input/output, hydration status, **vital signs hourly** |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > 03 Iv Fluid Resuscitation
text:
### **03 IV FLUID RESUSCITATION**

Use 0.9% NaCl (Normal Saline) as first-line. Switch to 0.45% NaCl in HHS once glucose <20 mmol/L and osmolality falling. Add 5% Dextrose when glucose <14 mmol/L (DKA) or <15 mmol/L (HHS) to allow continued insulin without hypoglycaemia.

text:
### **Potassium Safety Rules**

→ NEVER give undiluted KCl IV — fatal if bolused

→ Rates >20 mmol/hr require cardiac monitoring and central venous access

→ Initial K<sup>+</sup> may appear high/normal despite total body depletion — watch closely as insulin drives K<sup>+</sup> intracellularly

→ Hypokalaemia is the leading cause of preventable death in DKA

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Complications to Anticipate & Manage
text:
| Complication | Recognition | Management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cerebral Oedema | Declining GCS, headache, bradycardia after initial improvement | Reduce fluids; Mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg IV; Urgent transfer to higher level |
| Hypokalaemia | Commonest preventable death. ECG: U waves, ST depression, QT prolongation | Check K+ every 2 hrs, replace aggressively per protocol (Section 04) |
| Hypoglycaemia | Glucose falling too rapidly or <4 mmol/L | Add dextrose to fluids; NEVER stop insulin — reduce rate instead |
| Hyperchloraemic Acidosis | Non-anion gap acidosis despite DKA treatment, large NS volumes given | Switch to balanced crystalloid (Ringer’s Lactate) if available; reduce NS |
| Thromboembolism (HHS) | High risk in HHS — may be clinically silent | LMWH prophylaxis: enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily (no contraindication). TED stockings |
| Pulmonary Oedema | Crackles on auscultation, SpO2 falling, worsening dyspnoea | Reduce fluid rate; furosemide if fluid overloaded; CXR; oxygen |
| Acute Kidney Injury | Urine output <0.5 ml/kg/hr persisting after resuscitation | Ensure adequate fluids; avoid nephrotoxins; urgent nephrology review if severe |
| Infection / Sepsis | Fever, leukocytosis, clinical signs of source | Empirical antibiotics: co-amoxiclav or ceftriaxone; cultures before ABx; check HIV |

text:
Diagram: Algorithm for DKA (section: Algorithm for DKA)
Items: Immediate Assessment
- Clinic History Polyuria, Polydipsia, Nocturia, Enuresis Weight Loss Nausea, Vomiting, Abdominal Pain Weakness, Fatigue Confusion, Level of Consciousness -> Diagnosis confirmed Diabetes Ketoacodosis Contact Senior Staff
- Clinical Signs Dehydration Deep signing respiration (Kussmaul) Smell of ketones Lethargy/drowsiness -> Diagnosis confirmed Diabetes Ketoacodosis Contact Senior Staff
- Biochemical Features & Investigations Ketones in Urine Blood Glucose Acidemia (vpH < 7.3, HCO3 <15 mmol/L) Urea, electrolytes Other investigations as indicated -> Diagnosis confirmed Diabetes Ketoacodosis Contact Senior Staff
- Diagnosis confirmed Diabetes Ketoacodosis Contact Senior Staff -> Shock (reduced peripheral pulses) Reduced conscious level/coma; Dehydration >5% Not in shock Acidotic (hyperventilation) Vomiting; Minimal dehydration Tolerating oral fluid
- Shock (reduced peripheral pulses) Reduced conscious level/coma -> Resuscitation Airway ± NG tube Breathing (100% oxygen) Circulation (0.9% saline 10-20 ml/kg over 1-2 h & repeat until circulation is restored *See CE Management*
- Dehydration >5% Not in shock Acidotic (hyperventilation) Vomiting -> IV Therapy Saline 0.9% 10ml/kg over 1h; may repeat Calculated fluid requirements Correct fluid deficit over 24-48 hours ECG for abnormal T-waves Add KCl 40 mmol per liter fluid
- Minimal dehydration Tolerating oral fluid -> Therapy Start with SC insulin Continue oral hydration
- Resuscitation Airway ± NG tube Breathing (100% oxygen) Circulation (0.9% saline 10-20 ml/kg over 1-2 h & repeat until circulation is restored *See CE Management* -> IV Therapy Saline 0.9% 10ml/kg over 1h; may repeat Calculated fluid requirements Correct fluid deficit over 24-48 hours ECG for abnormal T-waves Add KCl 40 mmol per liter fluid
- Therapy Start with SC insulin Continue oral hydration -> No improvement
- No improvement -> IV Therapy Saline 0.9% 10ml/kg over 1h; may repeat Calculated fluid requirements Correct fluid deficit over 24-48 hours ECG for abnormal T-waves Add KCl 40 mmol per liter fluid
- IV Therapy Saline 0.9% 10ml/kg over 1h; may repeat Calculated fluid requirements Correct fluid deficit over 24-48 hours ECG for abnormal T-waves Add KCl 40 mmol per liter fluid -> Continuous insulin infusion at 0.05 – 0.1 unit /kg/hour starting 1 hour after fluids initiated
- Continuous insulin infusion at 0.05 – 0.1 unit /kg/hour starting 1 hour after fluids initiated -> Critical Observations Hourly blood glucose Hourly fluid input & output Neurological Status at least hourly Electrolytes 2 hourly after starting IV Fluid Therapy Monitor ECG for T-wave changes
- Critical Observations Hourly blood glucose Hourly fluid input & output Neurological Status at least hourly Electrolytes 2 hourly after starting IV Fluid Therapy Monitor ECG for T-wave changes -> Acidosis not improving; Blood glucose ≤17 mmol/L (300 mg/dL) or Blood glucose falls >5 mmol/L/hour (90 mg/dL); Neurological deterioration Warning Signs: Severe or progressive headache, slowing heart rate, irritability, confusion, decreased consciousness, incontinence, specific neurological signs
- Acidosis not improving -> Re-evaluate IV fluid calculations Insulin delivery system & dose Need for additional resuscitation. Consider sepsi
- Blood glucose ≤17 mmol/L (300 mg/dL) or Blood glucose falls >5 mmol/L/hour (90 mg/dL) -> IV Therapy Change to 0.45% or 0.9% saline; add glucose to fluids (5% - 12.5%) to prevent hypoglycemia Adjust sodium infusion to promote an increase in measured serum sodium
- Neurological deterioration Warning Signs: Severe or progressive headache, slowing heart rate, irritability, confusion, decreased consciousness, incontinence, specific neurological signs -> Exclude hypoglycemia is it cerebral edema?
- Exclude hypoglycemia is it cerebral edema? -> CE Management Give mannitol 0.5-1g/kg or 3% hypertonic saline Adjust IV fluids to maintain normal BP, but avoid over-hydration Call Senior Staff Move to ICU Consider cranial imaging only after patient stabilized
- IV Therapy Change to 0.45% or 0.9% saline; add glucose to fluids (5% - 12.5%) to prevent hypoglycemia Adjust sodium infusion to promote an increase in measured serum sodium -> Improved Clinically well, ketoacidosis resolved, tolerating oral fluids
- Improved Clinically well, ketoacidosis resolved, tolerating oral fluids -> Transition to SC Insulin Start SC insulin then stop IV insulin after an appropriate interval

narrative: Algorithm for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) (NCDIMH guidelines, page 50). Immediate assessment: history (polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, weakness, confusion), signs (dehydration, Kussmaul breathing, ketone smell, drowsiness) and investigations (urine ketones, blood glucose, acidaemia with pH below 7.3 or HCO3 below 15 mmol/L, urea and electrolytes). Once DKA is confirmed contact senior staff. Shock or reduced consciousness: resuscitate (airway, 100% oxygen, 0.9% saline 10-20 mL/kg over 1-2 hours, repeat until circulation restored), then IV therapy. Dehydration above 5%, not in shock, acidotic or vomiting: IV therapy with 0.9% saline 10 mL/kg over 1 hour, correct the deficit over 24-48 hours, ECG for T-waves, add KCl 40 mmol per litre, then continuous insulin infusion 0.05-0.1 unit/kg/hour starting 1 hour after fluids. Minimal dehydration tolerating oral fluids: SC insulin and oral hydration; if no improvement, IV therapy. Monitor hourly glucose, fluid balance and neurological status; electrolytes 2-hourly; ECG. If acidosis is not improving, re-evaluate fluids, insulin delivery and dose, and consider sepsis. If glucose is 17 mmol/L (300 mg/dL) or less, or falls more than 5 mmol/L/hour, change to 0.45% or 0.9% saline with 5-12.5% glucose. If neurological deterioration (headache, slow heart rate, irritability, confusion), exclude hypoglycaemia and manage cerebral oedema: mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg or 3% saline, avoid over-hydration, call senior staff, move to ICU, cranial imaging only after stabilisation. When improved, transition to SC insulin then stop IV insulin.

### **Key Notes:**

* Correction dose is ADDED to the scheduled (basal bolus) insulin dose.
* Bedtime correction doses apply to eating patients only; omit for NPO patients.
* “+ CALL” = notify prescriber immediately for clinical review.
* NPO patients: consider IV fluids and TPN; consult endocrinologist. Administer SC (subcutaneous) insulin only as directed.
* If hypoglycaemia occurs or is recurrent, step DOWN one sensitivity level (Resistant → Average → Sensitive).
* Reassess TDI and correction scale level daily based on glucose trends and clinical status.

text:
|  | Diabetes in Pregnancy | Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Definition | Pregnancy in a woman known to have pre-existing diabetes (Type 1 or Type 2), or hyperglycaemia first detected in pregnancy that meets WHO criteria for diabetes in the non-pregnant state | Hyperglycaemia first detected during pregnancy (usually in 2nd or 3rd trimester) that does not meet WHO criteria for diabetes in the non-pregnant state |
| Timing of Onset | May occur at any time, including the 1st trimester | Typically develops in the 2nd or 3rd trimes-ter |
| Underlying Type | Usually Type 1 or Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus | Pregnancy-induced glucose intolerance |
| Diagnostic Criteria (WHO / IADPSG) | Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) ≥ 7.0 mmol/L OR | Any one of the following (on 75 g OGTT): • Fasting: ≥ 5.1 mmol/L • 1-hour: ≥ 10.0 mmol/L • 2-hour: ≥ 8.5 mmol/L |
| Management Focus | 2-hour OGTT (75 g glucose) ≥ 11.1 mmol/L OR Random Plasma Glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L with symptoms | • Dietary modification and physical activity • Monitor blood glucose regularly and start on Metformin if glycaemic control not reached • Insulin therapy if lifestyle and Metformin measures fail • Postpartum screening for Type 2 DM |
| Postpartum Follow-Up | • Optimize pre-existing diabetes control before and during pregnancy • Frequent glucose monitoring • Adjust insulin regimen as needed • Fetal growth and anomaly surveillance | Reassess glycaemic status 6–12 weeks postpartum; repeat OGTT every year to detect Type 2 DM |

text:
| **Screening** | | | | --- | --- | --- | | During Pregnancy | • Healthy diet, regular exercise >> unless there are obstetric contraindications.
• Possible personalized gestational weight gain.
• High-risk women: detect early DM in pregnancy (if preconception positive screening)
• Follow the protocol for all at 24 to 28 weeks gestation according to recommended screening and diagnostic criteria.
• Delivery at 38 weeks is advised if the sugars are well controlled. If poorly controlled consult a specialist on timing of delivery.
• Consider steroid administration for lung maturation if early delivery is indicated.
• If steroids are administered at any point in the pregnancy, anticipate difficult glycaemic control and insulin therapy is advised.
• Aim target blood glucose level 4-7 mmol/L during active labour and delivery.
• Anticipate maternal and foetal/neonatal complications at delivery and plan for necessary interventions. | | | Postpartum | • Early postpartum OGTT to assess glucose status.
• Regular long-term follow-up focused on diabetes and cardiovascular risk factor modification.
• Family lifestyle support: optimizing diet, physical activity, and weight in the offspring. | |

text:
## Diabetes in Special Populations

| HIV/TB Co-infection | Resource-Limited Settings |
| --- | --- |
| - Screen for HIV if status unknown (rapid test on admission) - Immune reconstitution can unmask T1DM - ARVs (especially older PI-based) can cause insulin resistance - Opportunistic infections (PCP, cryptococcal, TB) are common DKA precipitants - Maintain ARTs during crisis - liaise with HIV team | - No blood ketones: use urine ketones (≥2+ = significant) - No VBG: treat on clinical picture + glucose + ketones - No syringe pump: 50 units in 500 ml NS (0.1 unit/ml) + drip control - No 0.45% NaCl: use 0.9% NaCl throughout with closer monitoring - Validate POC glucose meters for high glucose ranges >30 mmol/L |
| Pregnancy | Elderly Patients (HHS) |
| - DKA can occur at lower glucose (euglycaemic DKA in pregnancy) - Involve obstetric team immediately - Fetal monitoring from 24 weeks onwards - Higher insulin requirements - do not underdose - Avoid bicarbonate unless pH <7.0 | - Reduced physiological reserve - higher risk of fluid overload - More gradual fluid replacement over 48-72 hours - Increased thromboembolic risk - early LMWH prophylaxis - Exclude silent MI, stroke, UTI, pneumonia as precipitant - Assess cognition, falls risk, social support before discharge |

within 1 SD of the young adult reference mean (T-score\* at or above -1.0) | | **Low Bone mass** | BMD or BMC value more than 1 SD, but less than 2.5 (osteopenia) SD below the
young adult mean (T-score between -1.0 and - 2.5) | | **Osteoporosis** | BMD or BMC value is 2.5 SD or more below the young adult mean | | **Severe osteoporosis** | BMD or BMC value more than 2.5 SD below the young adult mean, plus one or more
fragility fractures | | **These criteria were updated in 2008 and differ from those proposed by the WHO in 1994 by specifying a
single reference site (the femoral neck) to measure BMD, providing a young normal reference range for
women and men (the NHANES III reference data for femoral neck measurements in women aged 20-29
years), and by accommodating diagnostic criteria for men (see 6.2.1 and 6.3).
\*\* When standard deviation (SD) units are used in relation to the young healthy adult population, this is
referred to as the T-score.** | |

## **Classification of Osteoporosis**

| **Definition** | **Criteria** |
| --- | --- |
| **Normal** | BMD or BMC value (measured with DXA at either the spine, total hip or femur neck) within 1 SD of the young adult reference mean (T-score\* at or above -1.0) |
| **Low Bone mass** | BMD or BMC value more than 1 SD, but less than 2.5 (osteopenia) SD below the young adult mean (T-score between -1.0 and - 2.5) |
| **Osteoporosis** | BMD or BMC value is 2.5 SD or more below the young adult mean |
| **Severe osteoporosis** | BMD or BMC value more than 2.5 SD below the young adult mean, plus one or more fragility fractures |
| **These criteria were updated in 2008 and differ from those proposed by the WHO in 1994 by specifying a single reference site (the femoral neck) to measure BMD, providing a young normal reference range for women and men (the NHANES III reference data for femoral neck measurements in women aged 20-29 years), and by accommodating diagnostic criteria for men (see 6.2.1 and 6.3). \*\* When standard deviation (SD) units are used in relation to the young healthy adult population, this is referred to as the T-score.** |  |

text:
\*Clinician may use any of the following procedures1:
1. **The Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre:** The patient sits at the edge of the bed and the examiner turns the patient’s head 30 - 45 degrees to the side being tested. The patient needs to keep their eyes open and focus on a stable point, and then quickly lie supine and hyperextend the neck. Horizontal nystagmus denotes a positive test. This test can induce vertigo, so patients should be warned about this before the test is performed.
2. **Orthostatic blood pressure testing:** A drop in the systolic blood pressure by more than 20 mm/Hg from a lying down to standing position is significant for a postural drop. This is seen in patients who are dehydrated or who present with autonomic dysfunction. Autonomic dysfunction can occur acutely and be driven by vertigo.
3. **Head impulse test:** The patient is asked to look at the examiner’s nose and the examiner quickly turns the patient’s head 10–20 degrees. It is abnormal if eyes move rapidly and repetitively, failing to re-fixate to the examiner’s nose. A positive test indicates disrupted vestibule-ocular reflex.

| Gastrointestinal & Voice | - Constipation - Hoarse voice |

narrative: Thyroid storm recognition and management (NCDIMH guidelines, page 82). Suspect thyroid storm if the Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale (BWPS) is 45 or more. Identify the precipitant(s). Initial stabilisation (airway, breathing, circulation) and give propylthiouracil (PTU) or methimazole. Then block thyroid hormone synthesis at least 1 hour after the antithyroid drug: Lugol's iodine 8 drops orally every 6-8 hours, or sodium iodide IV 0.25-0.5 g every 6 hours. Block peripheral effects: propranolol 60-80 mg orally every 6 hours or 1 mg IV every 10 minutes (maximum 3 doses), and hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 8 hours. Continuously monitor and support: ECG, vitals, fluid balance and electrolytes, and adjust therapy as needed.

narrative: Management of hyperthyroidism in pregnancy (NCDIMH guidelines, page 85). Two entry points. Known hyperthyroidism on antithyroid drugs (ATD) and wishing to conceive or pregnant: switch from a block-and-replace regimen to dose titration; use propylthiouracil (PTU) before conception and in the first trimester, then carbimazole (CBZ). New diagnosis during pregnancy: start PTU in the first trimester, CBZ thereafter. Both: refer to an endocrine physician, check thyroid function tests every 4 weeks (and liver function tests every 4 weeks if on PTU), and check TRAb at 22 and 36 weeks. If free T4 is above the normal range, increase the ATD dose; if at or just above the upper end of normal, continue the current dose; if below the upper end of normal, decrease the dose; then recheck thyroid function in 4 weeks. If TRAb is more than 2-3 times the upper limit of normal, do an obstetric ultrasound to monitor for fetal thyrotoxicosis. Check thyroid function 6-8 weeks postpartum at the first antenatal check.

Management of hyperthyroidism in pregnancy (NCDIMH guidelines, page 85). Two entry points. Known hyperthyroidism on antithyroid drugs (ATD) and wishing to conceive or pregnant: switch from a block-and-replace regimen to dose titration; use propylthiouracil (PTU) before conception and in the first trimester, then carbimazole (CBZ). New diagnosis during pregnancy: start PTU in the first trimester, CBZ thereafter. Both: refer to an endocrine physician, check thyroid function tests every 4 weeks (and liver function tests every 4 weeks if on PTU), and check TRAb at 22 and 36 weeks. If free T4 is above the normal range, increase the ATD dose; if at or just above the upper end of normal, continue the current dose; if below the upper end of normal, decrease the dose; then recheck thyroid function in 4 weeks. If TRAb is more than 2-3 times the upper limit of normal, do an obstetric ultrasound to monitor for fetal thyrotoxicosis. Check thyroid function 6-8 weeks postpartum at the first antenatal check.

text:
## How to measure blood pressure correctly

**Checklist:**
- No exercise, smoking, caffeine or food 30 min before
- Quiet environment
- Comfortable temperature
- 3-5 min rest before measurement
- No talking before or during measurements
- Take 3 measurements at 1 min intervals and use the average of the last two

# **Non-pharmacological Treatment**

- Reduce the use of drugs known to cause gastritis (e.g., NSAIDs, alcohol)
- Stop smoking
- Reduce fatty, spicy and deep-fried foods

text:

The priority is to stabilize vital signs. A structured approach to the assessment of airway, breathing, circulation, and disability (ABCD). The possibility of abusive head trauma in infants and children needs to be considered.

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Diagnosis of Epilepsy > Complications of Epilepsy
text:
# Complications of Epilepsy

- High mortality- sudden death, injury, and motor vehicle accidents.
- Fall- it might lead to fractures, head contusion or internal bleeding
- Dropout of school or unemployment
- Adverse effects or intoxication of AEDs

heading_path: Chapter 14: Pulmonology > Bronchiectasis
text:
## **Bronchiectasis**

Is dilation of the bronchi when their wall becomes inflamed, thickened and irreversibly damaged, usually following obstruction followed by infection. The left lower lobe and lingula are the commonest sites for localized disease.
